title: Propositions
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A proposition is a declarative statement of fact with a truth value — either true or false, never both. A false statement is still a proposition.

## Worked example
“5 is prime” is true; “8 is prime” is false. “3+x=5” has a free variable and is not yet a proposition; with x=1 it is a false proposition.

## Common mistake
Commands and questions do not assert a truth value.

## How it shows up on the test
Decide which sentences are propositions and justify truth values.

title: Negation
notes:
## Definition and key facts
¬p means “It is not the case that p” and reverses its truth value. Negate an inequality by including equality in the complement when needed.

## Worked example
¬(x<3) means x≥3; ¬(x>3) means x≤3; ¬(x≤3) means x>3; ¬(x≥3) means x<3.

## Common mistake
“Not younger” includes the same age.

## How it shows up on the test
Give a useful English negation without an ambiguous “not.”

title: Conjunction
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p∧q is the proposition of both p and q. Both must be true, false otherwise.

## Worked example
For TT, TF, FT, FF the column is T,F,F,F. “p but q” also means p∧q; “but” adds no new truth condition.

## Common mistake
Do not treat “but” as exclusive or.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate statements joined by and, but, or nevertheless.

title: Disjunction
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p∨q is true if at least one operand is true. Or is inclusive by default: one or the other or both.

## Worked example
For TT, TF, FT, FF the column is T,T,T,F. A prerequisite “Calc 2 or Comp 110” allows someone who has taken both.

## Common mistake
Inclusive or is true when both inputs are true.

## How it shows up on the test
Distinguish conjunction from inclusive disjunction.

title: Inclusive and exclusive or
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p⊕q is exclusive or: exactly one proposition is true, not both. In class, “either … or” is a cue to examine exclusivity; explicit “or both” overrides it.

## Worked example
For TT, TF, FT, FF, XOR is F,T,T,F. Spending all savings on a trip or a car is exclusive in the class example.

## Common mistake
Context matters; ordinary prose sometimes uses “either” inclusively.

## How it shows up on the test
Explain why a given everyday or permits or excludes both.

title: Conditional and English forms
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p→q is false only if p is true and q is false. p is the condition and q its result. “p only if q,” “q is necessary for p,” “p is sufficient for q,” “q whenever p,” and “q unless ¬p” all express p→q.

## Worked example
“I run whenever it is sunny”: let p=it is sunny, q=I run. Then p→q. The false case is sunny without running. For TT,TF,FT,FF: T,F,T,T.

## Common mistake
Only if points toward the necessary condition. A false hypothesis makes the implication true.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate a long hypothesis as one grouped conjunction, then identify its conclusion.

title: Biconditional
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p↔q means p if and only if q: (p→q)∧(q→p). It is true exactly when the inputs agree.

## Worked example
“You can fly iff you bought a ticket” is true when both happen or neither happens, and false when only one happens. TT,TF,FT,FF: T,F,F,T.

## Common mistake
One implication does not prove a biconditional.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate necessary and sufficient; check both directions.

title: Converse
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The converse of p→q is q→p. It reverses hypothesis and conclusion.

## Worked example
Original: if sunny, then I run. Converse: if I run, then sunny. With p=F,q=T, the original is true and the converse false.

## Common mistake
The converse is not generally equivalent to the original.

## How it shows up on the test
Write the converse of a compound English implication.

title: Inverse
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The inverse of p→q is ¬p→¬q. It negates both parts without swapping them.

## Worked example
If it is not sunny, then I do not run. The inverse and converse are contrapositives of one another and hence equivalent.

## Common mistake
Negate a compound hypothesis with De Morgan, not one word at a time.

## How it shows up on the test
Negate an and-hypothesis to an or-hypothesis.

title: Contrapositive
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The contrapositive of p→q is ¬q→¬p. It is the only one of converse, inverse, and contrapositive always equivalent to the original.

## Worked example
If I do not run, then it is not sunny. Both original and contrapositive fail precisely at p=T,q=F.

## Common mistake
Swap AND negate; doing only one operation gives the wrong statement.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate contrapositives and use this allowed equivalence in arguments.

title: Compound truth tables
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A truth table lists every assignment to its propositional variables. With n distinct variables it has 2ⁿ rows. Compute inner subexpressions before the outer connective.

## Worked example
For (p∨¬q)→(p∧q), use columns p,q,¬q,p∨¬q,p∧q,whole. In TT,TF,FT,FF order the result is T,F,T,F.

## Common mistake
Repeated occurrences of p do not add variables.

## How it shows up on the test
Build enough intermediate columns to make each row checkable.

title: Operator precedence
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Parentheses first; then ¬, ∧, ∨, →, ↔ in decreasing binding strength. Use parentheses when mixing XOR or chaining implications to avoid ambiguity.

## Worked example
¬p∨q∧r means (¬p)∨(q∧r). p∨q→r means (p∨q)→r.

## Common mistake
Negation acts only on the next formula unless parentheses enlarge its scope.

## How it shows up on the test
Parse a compound statement before building its truth table.

title: Tautology, contradiction, contingency
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A tautology is always true; a contradiction is always false; a contingency is true on some assignments and false on others.

## Worked example
p∨¬p is a tautology; p∧¬p is a contradiction; p→q is contingent because TF makes it false but TT makes it true.

## Common mistake
One true row does not establish a tautology.

## How it shows up on the test
Classify a compound statement using its full final column.

title: Logical equivalence
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p≡q means p↔q is a tautology. Prove this with matching truth-table columns or a chain of already-known equivalences.

## Worked example
p→q and ¬p∨q have the same T,F,T,T column. One mismatched row disproves an alleged equivalence.

## Common mistake
A rule of inference is one-way; equivalence is two-way.

## How it shows up on the test
Choose a counterexample row quickly when equivalence fails.

title: The only citable Table 7/8 identities
notes:
## Definition and key facts
All Table 6 identities are allowed. From Tables 7/8 ONLY: p→q≡¬p∨q (7.1); p→q≡¬q→¬p (contrapositive); p↔q≡(p→q)∧(q→p) (biconditional). Other identities must be derived.

## Worked example
To obtain ¬(p→q)≡p∧¬q: use 7.1, then DM, then DN. Do not cite this as an additional memorized Table 7 identity.

## Common mistake
A true identity may still be disallowed as a citation.

## How it shows up on the test
Label each substitution with an allowed law.

title: Successive substitution
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Write one equivalent expression per line, give the law that justifies the change, and end with ∎. Each substitution may replace a subexpression by an equivalent one.

## Worked example
¬(p→q) ≡ ¬(¬p∨q) [7.1]
≡ ¬¬p∧¬q [DM]
≡ p∧¬q [DN] ∎

## Common mistake
Do not replace implication with conjunction without negating the whole implication.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove an equivalence without a truth table.

title: Tautologies by equivalences
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove a tautology by equivalences, reduce the expression to T using only allowed laws.

## Worked example
(p∧q)→(p∨q) ≡ ¬(p∧q)∨(p∨q) [7.1]
≡ (¬p∨¬q)∨(p∨q) [DM]
≡ (p∨¬p)∨(q∨¬q) [comm, assoc]
≡ T∨T [negation]
≡ T [domination] ∎

## Common mistake
A chain must finish at T, not merely at a simpler contingent expression.

## How it shows up on the test
Recognize complementary terms after expanding conditionals.

title: Identity law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∧ T ≡ p; p ∨ F ≡ p. The neutral truth value leaves p unchanged.

## Worked example
p ∧ T ≡ p [Identity]
p ∨ F ≡ p [Identity]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Domination law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ T ≡ T; p ∧ F ≡ F. A true disjunct or false conjunct determines the result.

## Worked example
p ∨ T ≡ T [Domination]
p ∧ F ≡ F [Domination]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Idempotent law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ p ≡ p; p ∧ p ≡ p. Repeating a proposition adds no information.

## Worked example
p ∨ p ≡ p [Idempotent]
p ∧ p ≡ p [Idempotent]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Double negation law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
¬¬p ≡ p. Two negations cancel.

## Worked example
¬¬p ≡ p [Double negation]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Commutative law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p; p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p. Swap operands of the same connective.

## Worked example
p ∨ q ≡ q ∨ p [Commutative]
p ∧ q ≡ q ∧ p [Commutative]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Associative law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∨ r; p ∧ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∧ r. Regroup all ands or all ors.

## Worked example
p ∨ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∨ r [Associative]
p ∧ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∧ r [Associative]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Distributive law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r); p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r). Think of ands with ors; both distributive patterns are valid.

## Worked example
p ∨ (q ∧ r) ≡ (p ∨ q) ∧ (p ∨ r) [Distributive]
p ∧ (q ∨ r) ≡ (p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ r) [Distributive]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: De Morgan law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q; ¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q. Negate each piece and flip the connective.

## Worked example
¬(p ∧ q) ≡ ¬p ∨ ¬q [De Morgan]
¬(p ∨ q) ≡ ¬p ∧ ¬q [De Morgan]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Absorption law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p; p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p. The standalone p absorbs the more complicated term.

## Worked example
p ∨ (p ∧ q) ≡ p [Absorption]
p ∧ (p ∨ q) ≡ p [Absorption]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Negation law (Table 6)
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∨ ¬p ≡ T; p ∧ ¬p ≡ F. A proposition and its negation exhaust the possibilities.

## Worked example
p ∨ ¬p ≡ T [Negation law]
p ∧ ¬p ≡ F [Negation law]
Example: substitute (r→s) for p everywhere; each identity still holds for this compound proposition.

## Common mistake
Do not change connectives or drop parentheses beyond the stated pattern.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify the law or cite it in a successive-substitution proof.

title: Predicates and propositional functions
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The predicate is the property or relationship part of a sentence; the subject is what it is about. A propositional function P(x) depends on an input that can change.

## Worked example
For x>3, x is the subject and “is greater than 3” the predicate. P(4) is true. Q(x,y):x+y=3 gives Q(3,0)=T and Q(3,2)=F.

## Common mistake
Input order matters for x>y, even though it does not for x+y=3.

## How it shows up on the test
Evaluate a predicate after substituting all inputs.

title: Domains
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The domain is the allowed set of inputs. Stipulations on the subject are part of the meaning of a quantified statement.

## Worked example
∀x(x²≥x) is false over ℝ since x=1/2 fails, but true over ℤ: n≤0 or n≥1, so n(n−1)≥0.

## Common mistake
Never silently change ℝ into ℤ. ℕ includes 0.

## How it shows up on the test
Compare truth over ℝ, ℤ, ℕ, and ℤ⁺.

title: Universal quantification
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The universal quantification of P(x) says: for every x in the domain, P(x) is true. Notation ∀x∈D P(x).

## Worked example
∀x∈ℝ(x+1>x) is true because adding 1 increases every real number. One arbitrary x must suffice for a proof.

## Common mistake
Checking a few values is not proof for an infinite domain.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove a universal assertion or exhibit a counterexample.

title: Existential quantification
notes:
## Definition and key facts
There exists some (at least one) x in the domain so that P(x) is true: ∃xP(x).

## Worked example
Over ℤ, ∃x(x>3) is true with witness 4. ∃x(x=x+1) is false because subtracting x would give 0=1.

## Common mistake
An existential assertion does not mean exactly one.

## How it shows up on the test
Supply a witness and check that it belongs to the domain.

title: Counterexamples
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A counterexample to ∀xP(x) is a domain element a with P(a) false. To refute ∃xP(x), show every candidate fails.

## Worked example
∀x∈ℤ(x²>0) fails at x=0. That same example works over ℕ because 0∈ℕ.

## Common mistake
A number outside the specified domain cannot be a counterexample.

## How it shows up on the test
Find the simplest value, often 0, 1, −1, or 1/2.

title: Bound and free variables
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A variable occurrence is bound when it falls in the scope of its matching quantifier; otherwise it is free. A statement with a free variable need not have a fixed truth value.

## Worked example
In ∀x(P(x,y)→Q(x)), x is bound and y is free. In (∀xP(x))∨Q(x), the x in Q(x) is free.

## Common mistake
Scope is controlled by parentheses, not just a variable name appearing somewhere after a quantifier.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify free occurrences and parenthesize scope.

title: Quantifier distribution: two laws, two failures
notes:
## Definition and key facts
∀x(P∧Q) ≡ ∀xP∧∀xQ; ∃x(P∨Q) ≡ ∃xP∨∃xQ. But ∀x(P∨Q) ≢ ∀xP∨∀xQ, and ∃x(P∧Q) ≢ ∃xP∧∃xQ.

## Worked example
Let D={1,2}, P(x):x=1, Q(x):x=2. Everyone satisfies P or Q, but neither holds for everyone. Each predicate has a witness, but no single element satisfies both.

## Common mistake
In ∃x(P∧Q), it must be the same x; separate existential witnesses could be different.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove the valid distributions in words and refute the others with a two-element domain.

title: Negating quantified statements
notes:
## Definition and key facts
¬∀xP(x) ≡ ∃x¬P(x); ¬∃xP(x) ≡ ∀x¬P(x). Flip the quantifier, negate the inside.

## Worked example
¬∀x(x²>x) ≡ ∃x(x²≤x). ¬∃x(x²=2) ≡ ∀x(x²≠2). Negating “every student took Calc 2” gives “some student did not.”

## Common mistake
“Not every” means some do not, not none do.

## How it shows up on the test
Negate the formula, then translate back to natural English.

title: One-quantifier translations
notes:
## Definition and key facts
State the domain and define each predicate first. All A are B becomes ∀x(A(x)→B(x)); some A are B becomes ∃x(A(x)∧B(x)).

## Worked example
Domain people; S(x):x is a student, H(x):x is here. “Some students are absent” is ∃x(S(x)∧¬H(x)). With domain restricted to students it is ∃x¬H(x).

## Common mistake
Using implication under ∃ can make an unrelated nonstudent a witness.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate in both directions and negate without leaving a leading ¬.

title: Nested quantifiers
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A quantifier is nested when it falls in the scope of another. Predicates with multiple inputs allow one quantifier per variable.

## Worked example
Let P(x,y):x+y=0 over ℝ. Q(x)=∃yP(x,y) is a propositional function of x; ∀xQ(x) binds that remaining input.

## Common mistake
Count free variables after each quantifier is applied.

## How it shows up on the test
Read the sentence from the outermost quantifier inward.

title: Quantifier order
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Same-kind quantifiers commute: ∀x∀y and ∃x∃y can be swapped. Mixed quantifiers cannot generally be swapped. ∃y∀xP(x,y) implies ∀x∃yP(x,y).

## Worked example
Over ℝ, ∀x∃y(x+y=0) is true with y=−x. ∃y∀x(x+y=0) is false: x=−y+1 defeats any fixed y.

## Common mistake
A witness chosen first must work for every later universal choice.

## How it shows up on the test
Justify truth with a dependent witness or defeat every proposed fixed witness.

title: Truth values of the four nests
notes:
## Definition and key facts
For x+y=0 over ℝ: ∀∀ false, ∀∃ true, ∃∀ false, ∃∃ true. The justification matters as much as the letters.

## Worked example
∀∀ fails at x=y=1. ∀∃: choose y=−x. ∃∀ fails by choosing y=1−x. ∃∃: choose x=y=0. For xy=1 over ℝ, ∀∃ is false at x=0. For x<y, ∀∃ is true using y=x+1.

## Common mistake
A change to ℕ removes negative witnesses; x+y=0 then works only at (0,0).

## How it shows up on the test
Evaluate several nests over different domains.

title: Nested translations
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Specify each variable domain and predicate before translating. Universal choices come before witnesses that may depend on them.

## Worked example
Domain ℤ⁺: “sum of two positive integers is positive” is ∀x∀y(x+y>0). Domain ℤ: ∀x∀y((x>0∧y>0)→x+y>0).

## Common mistake
Restricting the domain can replace a condition inside the formula, but both forms must mean the same thing.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate mathematical and people/course statements.

title: Exactly one: existence and uniqueness
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Exactly one combines existence with the requirement that every other candidate equals the witness. For P: ∃x(P(x)∧∀z(P(z)→z=x)).

## Worked example
Domain people; B(x,y):x is best friends with y. Step 1: ∀x∃yB(x,y). Step 2: ∀x∃y(B(x,y)∧∀z(B(x,z)→z=y)).

## Common mistake
∀z(B(x,z)→z=y) alone allows no friends; it needs the existence clause.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate exactly one teacher or a unique person everybody can fool.

title: Negating nested statements
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Push negation inward one quantifier at a time, preserving their order while flipping each. Then negate the predicate or connective.

## Worked example
¬∀x∃y(x+y=0) ≡ ∃x¬∃y(x+y=0) [quantifier negation]
≡ ∃x∀y(x+y≠0) [quantifier negation] ∎

## Common mistake
Do not reverse the order of variables when flipping quantifiers.

## How it shows up on the test
Produce a useful negation with no leading ¬.

title: Vacuous truth on the practice sheet
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The sheet combines dependent witnesses, changing domains, and uniqueness. Its limit question was crossed out and is omitted.

## Worked example
∀x∀y∃z(x+y=z) is true over ℝ: choose z=x+y. ∃z∀x∀y(x+y=z) is false: (0,0) and (1,0) demand different z. “A student none of whose distinct friends are friends” need not have any friends.

## Common mistake
Do not accidentally add existence of two friends to a universal implication about pairs of friends.

## How it shows up on the test
Expect multi-part translation and negation questions like the homework.

title: Argument, premises, conclusion
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An argument is a sequence of propositions called premises, followed by a conclusion. An argument form replaces particular statements by propositional variables.

## Worked example
“If you have the password, you can log on; you have the password; therefore you can log on” has form p→q, p, ∴q.

## Common mistake
Identify entire propositions as atoms rather than splitting their English subject and predicate.

## How it shows up on the test
Extract premises and conclusion before starting a proof.

title: Validity is about the form
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An argument is valid if the truth of all premises implies the truth of the conclusion. Equivalently, (p₁∧…∧pₙ)→q is a tautology. It may have false premises.

## Worked example
The class example √2>3/2 ⇒ 2>9/4; √2>3/2; therefore 2>9/4 is valid MP, but its numerical premise is false.

## Common mistake
Validity alone does not certify that the premises or conclusion are actually true.

## How it shows up on the test
Separate the logical form from factual truth.

title: Step / Reason tables
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Write each premise or derived statement as a numbered step, with a reason referencing earlier steps. End with ∎.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① ¬s∧c | prem. |
| ② ¬s | simplification of ① |
| ③ w→s | prem. |
| ④ ¬w | M.T. of ③,② |
| ⑤ ¬w→n | prem. |
| ⑥ n | M.P. of ⑤,④ |
| ⑦ n→t | prem. |
| ⑧ t | M.P. of ⑦,⑥ |
∎

## Common mistake
Do not cite a conclusion before it has been established.

## How it shows up on the test
Construct a table for a 4–6 premise argument.

title: Equivalences inside arguments
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Logical equivalences go both ways; rules of inference go one way. An allowed equivalence may replace a statement inside a derivation.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① e→p | prem. |
| ② ¬e→z | prem. |
| ③ z→r | prem. |
| ④ ¬p→¬e | contrapositive of ① (log. equiv.) |
| ⑤ ¬e→r | Hypo. Syl. ②,③ |
| ⑥ ¬p→r | Hypo. Syl. ④,⑤ |
∎

## Common mistake
A converse is not an allowed replacement for an implication.

## How it shows up on the test
Use contraposition to connect the needed antecedent to a chain.

title: Showing invalidity
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An argument form is invalid when some truth assignment makes every premise true and the conclusion false. One such row suffices.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p=F, q=T | chosen assignment |
| ② p→q=T and q=T | evaluate premises |
| ③ p=F | conclusion false |
∎ Thus p→q,q,∴p is invalid.

## Common mistake
A false premise does not disprove validity.

## How it shows up on the test
Give a concrete counterexample assignment.

title: Two fallacies
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Affirming the conclusion: p→q, q, ∴p. Denying the hypothesis: p→q, ¬p, ∴¬q. Both are invalid.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p=F, q=T | counterexample for both forms |
| ② p→q=T; q=T; ¬p=T | all relevant premises true |
| ③ p=F; ¬q=F | the respective conclusions are false |
∎

## Common mistake
Do not confuse affirming q with MP, or denying p with MT.

## How it shows up on the test
Name the fallacy and demonstrate a counterexample.

title: Proving an inference rule
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To verify a rule, make the conjunction of its premises imply its conclusion and show the result is a tautology.

## Worked example
[(p→q)∧p]→q ≡ [(¬p∨q)∧p]→q [7.1]
≡ [(¬p∧p)∨(q∧p)]→q [dist]
≡ [F∨(q∧p)]→q [negation]
≡ (q∧p)→q [identity]
≡ ¬(q∧p)∨q [7.1]
≡ (¬q∨¬p)∨q [DM]
≡ (¬q∨q)∨¬p [comm, assoc]
≡ T∨¬p [negation]
≡ T [domination] ∎

## Common mistake
F∨X=X uses identity, correcting the ambiguous “dom.” note in the transcription.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove MP or another propositional rule using allowed equivalences.

title: Modus ponens
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p→q; p ∴ q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p→q | prem. |
| ② p | prem. |
| ③ q | M.P. of ①,② |
∎

## Common mistake
The rule cannot be run backward; an inferred conclusion does not restore the premises.

## How it shows up on the test
Recognize this pattern with compound statements substituted for variables.

title: Modus tollens
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p→q; ¬q ∴ ¬p. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p→q | prem. |
| ② ¬q | prem. |
| ③ ¬p | M.T. of ①,② |
∎

## Common mistake
The rule cannot be run backward; an inferred conclusion does not restore the premises.

## How it shows up on the test
Recognize this pattern with compound statements substituted for variables.

title: Hypothetical syllogism
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p→q; q→r ∴ p→r. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p→q | prem. |
| ② q→r | prem. |
| ③ p→r | Hypo. Syl. ①,② |
∎

## Common mistake
The rule cannot be run backward; an inferred conclusion does not restore the premises.

## How it shows up on the test
Recognize this pattern with compound statements substituted for variables.

notes:
## Definition and key facts
p∨q; ¬p ∴ q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p∨q | prem. |
| ② ¬p | prem. |
| ③ q | Disj. Syl. ①,② |
∎

## Common mistake

Recognize this pattern with compound statements substituted for variables.

title: Addition
notes:
## Definition and key facts
p ∴ p∨q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p | prem. |
| ② p∨q | Addition of ① |
∎

notes:

p∧q ∴ p. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

| ② p | simplification of ① |
∎

notes:
## Definition and key facts
p; q ∴ p∧q. This inference preserves truth: whenever all listed premises are true, the conclusion is true.

| ② q | prem. |

notes:

## Worked example
| Step | Reason |
| ① p∨q | prem. |

title: Vocabulary of proofs
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A theorem is a fact that can be proven true (main fact). A proposition is a theorem of lesser prominence (supporting details). An axiom is assumed without proof; a proof establishes truth by valid reasoning.

## Worked example
A lemma supports another proof; a corollary follows directly from a theorem; a conjecture is proposed but not proved. The odd-cube fact is a lemma in the ∛2 proof.

## Common mistake
“Proposition” here can mean a less prominent theorem, unlike its truth-valued-sentence meaning in 1.1.

## How it shows up on the test
Use precise vocabulary and justify unproved facts you rely on.

title: Direct proof
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove p→q directly, suppose p is true and use definitions and algebra to establish q.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose n is odd. Then there exists some integer k so that n=2k+1. Now n²=4k²+4k+1=2(2k²+2k)+1. Since 2k²+2k∈ℤ, n² is odd. ∎

## Common mistake
A few numerical examples are not a proof for every integer.

## How it shows up on the test
Open with Suppose and introduce integer witnesses explicitly.

title: Even integers
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An integer n is even if there exists some integer k so that n=2k.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose n=2k with k∈ℤ. Then n²=4k²=2(2k²). Since 2k²∈ℤ, n² is even. ∎

## Common mistake
The witness must be an integer; every real number is twice another real number.

## How it shows up on the test
Show a quantity has the form 2 times an integer.

title: Odd integers and odd squares
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An integer n is odd if there exists some integer k so that n=2k+1. Every integer is either even or odd.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose n is odd. Then there exists some integer k so that n=2k+1. Now n²=2(2k²+2k)+1. Since 2k²+2k∈ℤ, n² is odd. ∎

## Common mistake
Do not write n=2k unless you are assuming evenness.

## How it shows up on the test
Reproduce the class’s canonical odd-square proof.

title: Perfect squares
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An integer n is a perfect square if there exists an integer k so that n=k².

## Worked example
Pf Suppose m,n are perfect squares. Then there exist integers k,j with m=k² and n=j². Now mn=k²j²=(kj)². Since kj∈ℤ, mn is a perfect square. ∎

## Common mistake
Use independent witnesses k,j for independent perfect squares.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove closure of perfect squares under multiplication.

title: Rational and irrational
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A real number x is rational if x=p/q for integers p,q with q≠0. An irrational real is not rational.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose x=p/q and y=a/b with integers p,q,a,b and q,b≠0. Then x+y=(pb+aq)/(qb). The numerator and denominator are integers and qb≠0, so x+y is rational. ∎

## Common mistake
The denominator condition must be stated. An irrational number is still real.

## How it shows up on the test
Write closure proofs using two separate fractions.

title: Contraposition: 3n+2
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove p→q, first state C.P.: If ¬q then ¬p. Then prove that implication directly.

## Worked example
C.P.: If n is even, then 3n+2 is even.
Pf We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose n is even; then there exists k∈ℤ with n=2k. Now 3n+2=2(3k+1). Since 3k+1∈ℤ, 3n+2 is even. ∎

## Common mistake
Negate both sides and swap their positions.

## How it shows up on the test
Use contraposition when the negated conclusion has a convenient definition.

title: At least one small factor
notes:
## Definition and key facts
If n=ab with positive integers a,b, then a≤√n or b≤√n. The conclusion is an inclusive or.

## Worked example
C.P.: If a>√n and b>√n, then n≠ab.
Pf We will prove the contrapositive. Suppose a>√n and b>√n. Positivity gives ab>√n·√n=n, hence ab≠n. ∎

## Common mistake
The handout’s “and” is a typo; a=1,b=9,n=9 refutes the and-version.

## How it shows up on the test
Negate an or-conclusion with De Morgan.

title: Contradiction of a proposition
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove p, assume ¬p and derive a contradiction r∧¬r. Name the contradiction at the end.

## Worked example
In the √2 proof, r is “p/q is reduced.” Deducing both p and q even gives ¬r, because 2 is a common factor.

## Common mistake
Assuming p itself would be circular reasoning.

## How it shows up on the test
Use the exact opening: assume for the sake of contradiction.

title: Canonical proof: √2 irrational
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Use a reduced fraction, then show both numerator and denominator are even. The parity lemma follows by contraposing the odd-square proof.

## Worked example
Pf We will prove this by contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that √2 is rational. Then there exist p,q∈ℤ, q≠0, with √2=p/q. We can assume p/q is reduced so p and q share no common factors. Squaring gives 2q²=p², so p² is even. Thus p is even; let p=2k with k∈ℤ. Then 2q²=4k², hence q²=2k² is even. Thus q is even. Both p and q have factor 2, contradicting that the fraction is reduced. ∎

## Common mistake
Do not assume p even merely because p² is even without mentioning the established parity lemma.

## How it shows up on the test
Reproduce this starred class proof accurately.

title: Contradiction of an implication
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove p→q by contradiction, assume both p and ¬q. This is the negation of the whole implication.

## Worked example
For irrational x and rational y, assume x+y rational. Write y=p/q, x+y=w/z with integer numerators/denominators and q,z≠0. Then x=(wq−pz)/(qz), rational — contradicting the hypothesis. ∎

## Common mistake
Assuming only ¬p or only ¬q loses necessary information.

## How it shows up on the test
Use rationality of a proposed sum to force rationality of an irrational summand.

title: Canonical proof: irrational plus rational
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The sum of an irrational and a rational is irrational.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose x is irrational and y is rational. We will prove this by contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that x+y is rational. There exist integers p,q,w,z with q,z≠0, y=p/q, and x+y=w/z. Then x=(wq−pz)/(qz). Since wq−pz,qz∈ℤ and qz≠0, x is rational, contradicting the hypothesis. ∎

## Common mistake
Two irrationals need not have irrational sum: √2+(−√2)=0.

## How it shows up on the test
Distinguish the true mixed-sum theorem from false claims about two irrationals.

title: Proving biconditionals
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To prove p↔q, prove both p→q and q→p, labeled (→) and (←). Different methods may be used for the directions.

## Worked example
Pf (→) Suppose n=2k+1. Then n²=2(2k²+2k)+1 is odd. (←) We prove the contrapositive: suppose n=2k. Then n²=2(2k²) is even. The integer witnesses justify both parity conclusions. Thus n is odd iff n² is odd. ∎

## Common mistake
Repeating the same direction in different words does not establish the converse.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove an iff about parity.

title: TFAE cycle
notes:
## Definition and key facts
To show several statements are equivalent, prove a cycle p₁→p₂→p₃→p₁. Transitivity then supplies every remaining direction.

## Worked example
Pf For n∈ℤ: (a) n even → (b) n−1 odd: n=2k gives n−1=2(k−1)+1. (b)→(c) n² even: n−1=2k+1 gives n²=4(k+1)²=2[2(k+1)²]. (c)→(a): contrapose; odd n has odd square by the class proof. Each bracketed witness is an integer. ∎

## Common mistake
A chain without the final link back to the start is insufficient.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove three equivalent conditions efficiently.

title: Canonical proof: ∛2 irrational
notes:
## Definition and key facts
First prove the lemma n³ even ⇒ n even by contraposition; then repeat the reduced-fraction contradiction.

## Worked example
Lemma: if n=2k+1, then n³=8k³+12k²+6k+1=2(4k³+6k²+3k)+1, odd. Pf We will prove this by contradiction. Assume for the sake of contradiction that ∛2=p/q in lowest terms, p,q∈ℤ, q≠0. Then 2q³=p³, so p³ is even and the lemma gives p=2k. Hence q³=4k³=2(2k³), even; the lemma gives q even. Both p and q have factor 2, contradicting lowest terms. ∎

## Common mistake
The square-parity lemma alone does not justify the cube step; establish the cube lemma.

## How it shows up on the test
Adapt the √2 structure while carefully changing exponents.

title: Sets and elements
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A set is an unordered collection of distinct objects which we call elements. x∈A means x is an element; x∉A means it is not.

## Worked example
{1,3,5}={5,1,3,1}. Reordering and repeating elements do not change a set. {ℕ,ℤ,ℚ,ℝ} has four elements, each of which is itself a set.

## Common mistake
Distinguish the objects inside outer braces from their own contents.

## How it shows up on the test
Read nested sets carefully and ignore duplicate elements.

title: Roster, set-builder, intervals
notes:
## Definition and key facts
Roster notation lists elements. Set-builder notation describes exactly which objects qualify. Interval notation describes real numbers between endpoints.

## Worked example
{1,3,…,99}={x∈ℤ : x is odd and 1≤x≤99}. (a,b]={x∈ℝ : a<x≤b}; [a,b] includes both endpoints, (a,b) includes neither.

## Common mistake
An interval contains real numbers, not just the displayed integer endpoints.

## How it shows up on the test
Translate between notation styles and test endpoints.

title: Standard number sets
notes:
## Definition and key facts
ℕ={0,1,2,…}, ℤ={…,−1,0,1,…}, ℤ⁺={1,2,…}; ℚ rational, ℚ⁺ positive rational, ℝ real, ℝ⁺ positive real, ℂ complex. ℕ includes 0 in this class.

## Worked example
ℤ⁺⊂ℕ⊂ℤ⊂ℚ⊂ℝ⊂ℂ. Also ℤ⁺⊂ℚ⁺⊂ℝ⁺⊂ℝ and ℚ⁺⊂ℚ. √2∈ℝ but √2∉ℚ.

## Common mistake
ℝ⁺ excludes 0; ℕ does not.

## How it shows up on the test
Identify memberships and subset relationships among standard sets.

title: Empty set and singleton
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The empty set ∅={} is the only set with no elements. A singleton has exactly one element.

## Worked example
|∅|=0 but |{∅}|=1. {x∈ℤ:x²=1 and x>0}={1}, a singleton.

## Common mistake
Braces add a new set level: {∅} is not empty.

## How it shows up on the test
Distinguish zero elements from one empty-set element.

title: Set equality
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A=B iff every element of A is in B and every element of B is in A; equivalently A⊆B and B⊆A.

## Worked example
{1,1,3,3,5,5} and {3,1,5,1} equal {1,3,5}. {∅,1,3,5} does not, since it contains ∅. {{1},{3},{5}} does not, since its elements are sets.

## Common mistake
Equal cardinality does not imply equal sets.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove equality by two subset inclusions or disprove it with one differing element.

title: Universal set
notes:
## Definition and key facts
The universal set U contains all objects currently under consideration. It depends on the problem context.

## Worked example
When studying students in a class, U may be that class. In an interval problem, U is commonly ℝ. The universe for subsets of {0,1,2} can be {0,1,2}.

## Common mistake
Do not assume one universal set for every problem.

## How it shows up on the test
State the relevant universe when using set-builder notation.

title: Subset, superset, subset proofs
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A⊆B means ∀x(x∈A→x∈B). B⊇A says the same thing. To prove A⊆B, choose arbitrary x∈A and show x∈B.

## Worked example
Pf Suppose x∈{2k:k∈ℤ}. Then x=2k for some integer k, so x∈ℤ. Hence the even integers form a subset of ℤ. ∎ To disprove an inclusion, give x in A but outside B.

## Common mistake
A∈B and A⊆B make different claims: one concerns an element, one every element.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove a subset statement in the arbitrary-element format.

title: Proper subsets and supersets
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A⊂B (also A⊊B) means A⊆B and A≠B. Equivalently every element of A lies in B and some element of B lies outside A. B is a proper superset of A.

## Worked example
{1}⊂{1,2}, with witness 2 for strictness. A⊆A is true, but A⊂A is false.

## Common mistake
This app uses ⊂ strictly, following the class convention.

## How it shows up on the test
Prove the inclusion and exhibit an extra element.

title: ∅ ⊆ A and A ⊆ A
notes:
## Definition and key facts
For every set A, ∅⊆A and A⊆A. The first uses a vacuously true implication; the second uses reflexivity.

## Worked example
Pf There is no x∈∅ that could fail to lie in A, so every element of ∅ belongs to A. Also, if x∈A then x∈A, so A⊆A. ∎

## Common mistake
∅⊆A does not imply ∅∈A. For A={1}, only the subset statement holds.

## How it shows up on the test
Explain why empty-set inclusion needs no element witness.

title: Finite sets and cardinality
notes:
## Definition and key facts
A finite set has n distinct elements for some nonnegative integer n; its cardinality is |S|=n. A set that is not finite is infinite.

## Worked example
|{1,1,2}|=2; |{∅,{∅}}|=2; |{{1}}|=1; |∅|=0. ℕ is infinite even though it starts at 0.

## Common mistake
Count outermost distinct elements, not symbols or entries before removing duplicates.

## How it shows up on the test
Compute sizes of rosters and nested sets.

title: Power sets and 2ⁿ
notes:
## Definition and key facts
P(S) is the set of all subsets of S. If |S|=n then |P(S)|=2ⁿ: each element has two independent choices, included or omitted.

## Worked example
P({0,1,2})={∅,{0},{1},{2},{0,1},{0,2},{1,2},{0,1,2}}. P(∅)={∅}. P({∅})={∅,{∅}}.

## Common mistake
Include both ∅ and the original set; list subsets, not just elements.

## How it shows up on the test
List a small power set or compute its cardinality.

title: Nested sets
notes:
## Definition and key facts
An inner set is one element when it appears inside outer braces. Membership removes one brace level; subset compares elements without removing a level.

## Worked example
For A={{1}}, {1}∈A is true and 1∈A is false. {1}⊆A is false, since 1∉A. {{1}}⊆A is true because A⊆A.

## Common mistake
Do not flatten a nested set. ∅ and {∅} are different objects.

## How it shows up on the test
Judge ∈ and ⊆ statements involving ∅, {∅}, and {{1}}.

title: Choosing a proof method
notes:
## Definition and key facts
One-line rule: positive hypothesis → direct; negative or unhelpful hypothesis with a positive-when-negated conclusion → contraposition; a bare negative claim → contradiction; if-then with a negative conclusion that contraposition doesn't fix → contradiction of an implication; “iff” → both directions; “equivalent” → cycle; “prove or disprove” → try to break it first.

**Direct.** The hypothesis is a positive, unpackable property (even, odd, rational, perfect square, a | b) and the conclusion is positive too. You can write “there exists k so that …” immediately.

**Contraposition.** The hypothesis is hard to unpack but the negation of the conclusion is easy. Tells: the conclusion is “n is even/odd” while the hypothesis is about 3n + 2, n³ + 5, mn or n²; the conclusion is an “or” (its negation is an “and”); the hypothesis is “x is irrational” and the negated conclusion is a plain rational you can unpack (1/x, x/2).

**Contradiction of a proposition.** The statement is not an if-then and is a negative claim: “√2 is irrational”, “there is no rational r with …”, “there are no positive integers with …”. Tells: irrational, no, not, there is no, roots.

**Contradiction of an implication.** It is an if-then, the conclusion is negative, and contraposition would still leave a negative or irrational hypothesis to unpack: “if x is irrational and y is rational then x + y is irrational”; “if n is a perfect square then n + 2 is not”. Assume p and ¬q.

**Biconditional.** “If and only if”: prove (→) and (←), possibly by different methods.

**TFAE.** “Show these statements are equivalent” with three or more statements: prove a cycle.

**Counterexample.** “Prove or disprove” and the statement is false. When it is true, the answer is whichever method proves it, so test small examples first.

## Worked example
“If 3n + 2 is odd, then n is odd.” The hypothesis is about 3n + 2 and cannot be unpacked; the negated conclusion “n is even” gives n = 2k at once. Contraposition.

“If x is irrational and y is rational, then x + y is irrational.” If-then with a negative conclusion; contraposing gives “if x + y is rational then x is rational or y is irrational”, still awkward. Assume x irrational, y rational and x + y rational, then x = (x + y) − y is rational: contradiction of an implication.

## Common mistake
Reaching for contradiction because the word “irrational” appears, when the statement is an if-then whose negated conclusion unpacks cleanly (1/x irrational → contraposition). Also: forgetting to test examples on “prove or disprove” before writing a proof of a false statement.

## How it shows up on the test
The first line of every proof declares the method. Some statements admit two methods (n² even ⇒ n even works by contraposition or contradiction); either earns credit if executed cleanly.
